Divine Origins

Divine Origins is a comparative theology library. It compares creator gods, sacred texts and calendar systems across 15 tradition groups, with photographs of the real manuscripts, tablets and scrolls, and a Source Map that places 1403 deities from 252 traditions on one four-tier map of the divine (Source, Council, Demiurge, Archons, plus figures that cross tiers). Each tradition is described in its own voice, with scholarly context kept separate, and every claim is labelled as documented, debated or the tradition's own account.

Tradition groups (15)

  • Mesopotamian (c. 3500–539 BCE, Modern Iraq / Syria): The oldest written religious tradition. Cuneiform tablets from Uruk (c.3500 BCE) record the first named deities, the first flood narrative, the first dying god, and the first named author in human history.
  • Egyptian (c. 3100 BCE–400 CE, Northeast Africa (Nile Valley)): Among the most extensively documented ancient religions.
  • Canaanite / Ugaritic (c. 2000–200 BCE, Modern Israel, Lebanon, Syria): The direct predecessor of Hebrew monotheism.
  • Hebrew / Israelite (c. 1200 BCE–present, Ancient Israel / Judah): One of the most documented and studied religious traditions.
  • Ethiopian Orthodox (c. 330 CE (Christianization); traditions far older, Ethiopia / Eritrea / Horn of Africa): The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church preserves the most extensive Biblical canon (81 books).
  • Gnostic (c. 1st–4th century CE, Egypt · Syria · Roman Empire): A diverse family of religious movements that read the same scriptures as orthodox Christianity and Judaism — and drew radically different conclusions.
  • Christian (All Variants) (c. 30 CE–present, Global): Not one tradition but many — with dramatically different canons.
  • Greek / Roman / Hermetic (c. 800 BCE–400 CE, Mediterranean world): From Homer's Olympians to Plato's Demiurge to Plotinus's The One — Greek theology advanced in sophistication over a millennium.
  • Zoroastrian / Persian (c. 1500 BCE–present, Persia (modern Iran)): The first systematic eschatology in human religious history.
  • Hindu (c. 1500 BCE–present (continuous), India / South Asia): The oldest continuously practiced religion with identifiable roots.
  • Buddhist (c. 500 BCE–present, South / Southeast / East Asia; Global): Often described as non-theistic — but the Mahayana tradition's Dharmakaya (the luminous ground of consciousness that all beings share) is structurally equivalent to Brahman, The One, and Ain Soph.
  • East Asian (c. 600 BCE–present, China · Japan · Korea): The Tao Te Ching's "the Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao" is structurally equivalent to every mystical tradition's claim that the ultimate reality exceeds all language.
  • Norse / Celtic / Germanic (c. 800 BCE–1200 CE (documented), Scandinavia · British Isles · Germanic Europe): The Norse and Celtic traditions share deep structural parallels — both have all-father figures who preside over divine councils, dying-and-rising themes, a world-tree connecting realms, a catastrophic end of the world followed by renewal, a
  • African Traditions (Oral traditions; documented 19th–20th century CE, West Africa · North Africa · Diaspora (Americas)): Yoruba theology is among the most sophisticated in the world — 401 named Orishas, a complete divination system (Ifa Corpus), and a theology of the individual divine soul (Ori) that parallels the Gnostic divine spark.
  • Indigenous Traditions (Aboriginal: 60,000+ years; others: various, Americas · Pacific · Australia): The oldest spiritual tradition on Earth (Aboriginal Australian Dreaming, 60,000+ years) belongs to this group.

Sacred texts (57)

  • Sumerian King List (Mesopotamian, c. 2100 BCE): Lists kings who reigned before and after the Flood with reigns of tens of thousands of years.
  • Eridu Genesis (Sumerian Flood Story) (Mesopotamian, c. 2300 BCE (earliest fragments)): Oldest surviving flood narrative. Ziusudra (Utnapishtim) is warned by Enki of the coming flood.
  • Epic of Gilgamesh (Mesopotamian, c. 2100–1200 BCE (compiled)): The oldest surviving epic poem in world literature.
  • Enuma Elish (Mesopotamian, c. 1700 BCE): Seven tablets. Marduk defeats the chaos dragon Tiamat and creates the world from her body — heaven from one half, earth from the other.
  • Atrahasis Epic (Mesopotamian, c. 1700 BCE): Three tablets. Creation of humanity from clay mixed with divine blood so that gods could rest from labor.
  • Descent of Inanna to the Nether World (Mesopotamian, c. 2100 BCE): Oldest documented death-and-resurrection narrative.
  • Hymns to Inanna (Enheduanna) (Mesopotamian, c. 2285–2250 BCE): Written by Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad.
  • Pyramid Texts (Egyptian, c. 2400–2300 BCE): THE OLDEST RELIGIOUS TEXTS IN THE WORLD. Carved in hieroglyphs inside pyramids at Saqqara — first found in the Pyramid of Unas (c.2375 BCE).
  • Coffin Texts (Egyptian, c. 2100–1800 BCE): 1,185 spells painted inside coffins. Expanded from Pyramid Texts for non-royal use — democratizing the afterlife.
  • Book of the Dead (Pert em Hru) (Egyptian, c. 1550 BCE onward): Not one book but a collection of 192+ spells assembled individually for each deceased person.
  • Amduat ("What Is in the Duat") (Egyptian, c. 1500 BCE): 12 hours of Ra's night journey through the Duat (underworld).
  • Memphite Theology (Shabaka Stone) (Egyptian, c. 700 BCE (copies much older text)): Ptah creates the world through his heart (thought) and tongue (speech).
  • Torah (Five Books of Moses) (Hebrew / Israelite, c. 950–400 BCE (compiled)): Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy.
  • Dead Sea Scrolls — Deuteronomy 32 (4QDeut^j) (Hebrew / Israelite, c. 100–50 BCE (scroll); text much older): THE KEY TEXTUAL VARIANT. Standard Masoretic Text reads Deut 32:8: "according to the number of the sons of ISRAEL." The Dead Sea Scrolls version reads: "according to the number of the SONS OF GOD (bene elohim)." The Septuagint (Greek transla
  • Book of Enoch (1 Enoch) (Hebrew / Israelite, c. 300–100 BCE (various sections)): 108 chapters in 5 books. THE COMPLETE TEXT SURVIVES ONLY IN GE'EZ (Ethiopian).
  • Book of Jubilees (Hebrew / Israelite, c. 160–150 BCE): Retells Genesis through Exodus with additional detail.
  • Similitudes of Enoch (1 Enoch 37–71) (Hebrew / Israelite, c. 100 BCE–100 CE): Contains the figure of the "Son of Man" — a pre-existent heavenly being who will judge the world and sit on God's throne.
  • Dead Sea Scrolls (Complete Collection) (Hebrew / Israelite, c. 300 BCE–70 CE (texts); discovered 1947): 981 manuscripts discovered in 11 caves near Qumran, 1947–1956.
  • Sefer ha-Zohar (Book of Splendor) (Hebrew / Israelite, c. 1280–1286 CE (composed)): The central Kabbalistic text. Attributed to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (2nd century CE) but composed by Moses de León in medieval Spain — a claim established by Gershom Scholem in the 20th century.
  • Kebra Nagast (Glory of Kings) (Ethiopian Orthodox, c. 14th century CE (composed); oral tradition older): 117 chapters. Solomon and the Queen of Sheba (Makeda) unite; their son Menelik I is raised in Jerusalem, then travels with the firstborn sons of Israel's nobles.
  • Book of Enoch — Complete Ge'ez Text (Ethiopian Orthodox, c. 300–100 BCE (original); Ge'ez translation c. 4th–7th century CE): The ONLY complete surviving version of 1 Enoch.
  • Book of Meqabyan (3 Books) (Ethiopian Orthodox, Ethiopian tradition (date uncertain)): UNIQUE to the Ethiopian Orthodox canon. NOT the same as the Catholic/Orthodox Maccabees books.
  • Apocryphon of John (Secret Book of John) (Gnostic, c. 2nd century CE): THE central Sethian Gnostic text. 4 copies found at Nag Hammadi (II,1; III,1; IV,1; and the Berlin Codex BG 8502,2).
  • Nag Hammadi Library (Complete) (Gnostic, c. 2nd–4th century CE (texts); buried c. 367 CE): 52 texts in 13 leather-bound codices, discovered December 1945 in a clay jar near Nag Hammadi, Egypt — by farmers who were digging for fertilizer.
  • Gospel of Thomas (Gnostic, c. 50–140 CE): 114 sayings of Jesus. NO crucifixion. NO resurrection.
  • Pistis Sophia (Gnostic, c. 3rd–4th century CE): The Askew Codex. One of the longest surviving Gnostic texts — 4 books.
  • Timaeus (Plato) (Greek / Roman / Hermetic, c. 360 BCE): Plato's cosmological dialogue. The Demiurge (divine craftsman) looks to the eternal, unchanging Forms and shapes the material world after them.
  • Enneads (Plotinus) (Greek / Roman / Hermetic, c. 250 CE): 54 treatises in 6 groups of 9 (hence "Enneads").
  • Corpus Hermeticum (Greek / Roman / Hermetic, c. 100–300 CE): 17 tractates attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.
  • Gathas (17 Hymns of Zarathustra) (Zoroastrian / Persian, c. 1500–1000 BCE (estimated; debate ranges widely)): The oldest part of the Avesta. Attributed directly to Zarathustra (Zoroaster).
  • Rigveda (Hindu, c. 1500–1200 BCE): 1,028 hymns in 10 Mandalas (books). The oldest Veda.
  • Principal Upanishads (12–13 major) (Hindu, c. 800–200 BCE): "Sitting near the teacher." The philosophical foundation of all Hindu thought.
  • Bhagavad Gita (Hindu, c. 400–200 BCE): 18 chapters, 700 verses embedded in the Mahabharata (Book 6).
  • Prose Edda (Snorri Sturluson) (Norse / Celtic / Germanic, c. 1220 CE): The most complete source for Norse mythology, written by a Christian Icelander.
  • Völuspá (Prophecy of the Seeress) (Norse / Celtic / Germanic, c. 900–1000 CE (estimated composition)): 66 stanzas. A dead völva (seeress) addresses Odin and tells him the history and fate of the universe.
  • Ifa Corpus (Odu Ifa) (African Traditions, Oral tradition; codified 19th–20th century CE): 256 Odu (chapters), each containing thousands of verses (ese).
  • Popol Vuh (K'iche' Maya) (Indigenous Traditions, c. 1550 CE (written); oral tradition far older): THE definitive Maya creation narrative. Written down shortly after the Spanish conquest by K'iche' Maya nobles who learned the Latin alphabet.
  • Bardo Thodol (Tibetan Book of the Dead) (Buddhist, c. 8th century CE (attributed to Padmasambhava); revealed c. 14th century CE): The most elaborate death navigation manual in world religion.
  • Book of Breathings (Shemayim) (Egyptian, c. 4th century BCE – 2nd century CE): A late Egyptian funerary text — the successor to the Book of the Dead in the Ptolemaic and Roman periods.
  • Epic of Gilgamesh — Tablet XII (Death and the Underworld) (Mesopotamian, c. 2100–1200 BCE): Tablet XII is Mesopotamia's closest equivalent to a "Book of the Dead." Enkidu descends to the Underworld (Kur/Irkalla) and returns as a ghost to tell Gilgamesh what death is like.
  • Descent of Inanna — Death and Return (Mesopotamian, c. 2100 BCE): The oldest documented death-and-resurrection narrative.
  • Orphic Gold Tablets (Greek / Roman / Hermetic, c. 4th–3rd century BCE (earliest extant)): Small gold or bone tablets buried with the dead, containing instructions for navigating the afterlife — the Greek equivalent of the Egyptian Book of the Dead.
  • Myth of Er (Plato, Republic Book X) (Greek / Roman / Hermetic, c. 380 BCE): Plato's afterlife vision at the close of the Republic.
  • Aeneid Book VI — The Descent to the Underworld (Greek / Roman / Hermetic, c. 29–19 BCE): The most complete Roman afterlife cosmology.
  • Garuda Purana (Hindu, c. 800–1000 CE (compiled)): The Hindu equivalent of the Book of the Dead — traditionally recited in the presence of the dying and in the 13-day mourning period after death.
  • Katha Upanishad — Dialogue with Death (Hindu, c. 600–400 BCE): One of the most philosophically profound death texts in world literature.
  • Chinvat Bridge — The Zoroastrian Death Journey (Zoroastrian / Persian, c. 600 BCE (Gathas); elaborated in later texts): The Zoroastrian afterlife journey is among the oldest documented in world religion, predating most Greek and Hebrew elaborations.
  • Pistis Sophia — Afterlife Geography (Gnostic, c. 3rd–4th century CE): The most detailed Gnostic afterlife geography.
  • Norse Afterlife Cosmology (Hel, Valhalla, Niflheim) (Norse / Celtic / Germanic, c. 900–1220 CE (Eddic tradition)): The Norse tradition has no single "Book of the Dead" but a rich distributed afterlife cosmology across Eddic sources.
  • The Celtic Otherworld — Tír na nÓg, Annwn, the Sidhe (Norse / Celtic / Germanic, c. 700–1200 CE (documented); oral tradition older): The Celtic Otherworld is unique among afterlife cosmologies: it is not underground and not punishment-focused.
  • Jewish Afterlife Literature — Gehenna, Gan Eden, Sheol (Hebrew / Israelite, c. 200 BCE – 1000 CE (various)): Jewish afterlife theology evolved significantly over time.
  • Barzakh, the Grave, and the Islamic Afterlife Journey (Islamic Sufi, c. 610–632 CE (Quranic); c. 800–1000 CE (hadith elaboration)): The Islamic afterlife journey is documented across the Quran, Hadith, and theological writings.
  • Mictlan — The Aztec Underworld Journey (Indigenous Traditions, Pre-Conquest Mexica (Aztec) tradition; documented c. 1550 CE): The Aztec dead undertook a four-year journey through nine levels of the underworld to reach Mictlan — the deepest realm, ruled by Mictlantecuhtli and his consort Mictecacihuatl.
  • Xibalba — The Mayan Underworld (Popol Vuh) (Indigenous Traditions, c. 1550 CE (written); oral tradition c. 1000+ CE and earlier): Xibalba ("Place of Fright") is the Mayan underworld — one of the most elaborate death cosmologies in the Americas.
  • Orun — The Yoruba Afterlife and Ancestor World (African Traditions, Oral tradition; documented 19th–20th century CE): Yoruba afterlife theology is among the most sophisticated in the world.
  • Death and the Dreaming — Aboriginal Australian Death Journey (Indigenous Traditions, 60,000+ years (oral tradition)): There is no single Aboriginal death cosmology — hundreds of distinct language groups have their own traditions.
  • Ethiopian Orthodox Death Theology — Ge'ez Funerary Tradition (Ethiopian Orthodox, c. 4th century CE (Christianization of Ethiopia); texts compiled through 14th century CE): The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo tradition preserves a unique death theology shaped by its 81-book canon — including texts unavailable to Western Christianity.

Creator beings and divine archetypes (23)

  • An / Anu (Mesopotamian, c. 3500 BCE (earliest texts)): Highest god of the Sumerian pantheon. God of the heavens, sky, and stars.
  • Enki / Ea (Mesopotamian, c. 2600 BCE (earliest hymns)): God of wisdom, fresh water, magic, and creation.
  • Inanna / Ishtar (Mesopotamian, c. 3200 BCE (Uruk period)): Queen of Heaven and Earth. Goddess of love, war, and justice.
  • Tammuz / Dumuzi (Mesopotamian, c. 2600 BCE (earliest texts)): The shepherd-god. Consort of Inanna. Died and descended to the underworld annually, causing winter.
  • Marduk (Mesopotamian, c. 2000 BCE (Old Babylonian texts)): Supreme god of Babylon. Defeated the chaos dragon Tiamat and created the world from her body.
  • Ra / Amun-Ra / Atum (Egyptian, c. 2400 BCE (Pyramid Texts)): Supreme solar deity of Egypt. Self-created from the primordial waters of Nun.
  • Osiris (Egyptian, c. 2400 BCE (Pyramid Texts)): The original dying and rising god of Egyptian tradition.
  • Thoth / Hermes Trismegistus (Egyptian, c. 2400 BCE (Egyptian); c. 100-300 CE (Hermetic texts)): God of writing, wisdom, magic, the moon, and the dead.
  • El (Canaanite / Ugaritic, c. 1400 BCE (Ugaritic texts); earlier oral tradition): Supreme deity of the Canaanite pantheon. Father of all gods and humans.
  • El Elyon (Hebrew / Israelite, c. 1200 BCE (earliest Hebrew texts); earlier Canaanite tradition): The Most High God. In Deuteronomy 32:8-9 (Dead Sea Scrolls), El Elyon divides all nations among his divine sons — including assigning Israel to Yahweh.
  • Yahweh / YHWH (Hebrew / Israelite, c. 1200 BCE (earliest inscriptions); texts from c. 1000-400 BCE): God of Israel. Creator of heaven and earth.
  • Ain Soph (Hebrew / Israelite, c. 12th-13th century CE (textual Kabbalah); earlier mystical roots): The infinite, unknowable divine reality in Kabbalah.
  • The Monad (Gnostic, c. 1st-4th century CE (Gnostic texts)): The ultimate, unknowable, perfect source in Gnostic cosmology.
  • Yaldabaoth (Gnostic, c. 2nd century CE (Apocryphon of John)): The blind creator god of Gnostic cosmology.
  • Zeus / Jupiter (Greek / Roman / Hermetic, c. 800 BCE (Homer); earlier oral tradition): King of the Olympian gods. Presides over the divine council on Olympus.
  • The One (to Hen) (Greek / Roman / Hermetic, c. 250 CE (Plotinus, Enneads)): The ultimate principle in Neoplatonic philosophy.
  • Ahura Mazda (Zoroastrian / Persian, c. 1500-1000 BCE (Avestan texts; dating debated)): Supreme deity of Zoroastrianism. Uncreated, eternal, all-knowing, all-good.
  • Brahman (Hindu, c. 800-500 BCE (early Upanishads)): The ultimate, impersonal, all-pervading reality in Hindu philosophy.
  • Odin / All-Father (Norse / Celtic / Germanic, c. 900-1100 CE (Eddas); earlier oral tradition): Supreme Norse deity. All-Father. God of wisdom, war, death, magic, poetry, and runes.
  • The Tao (East Asian, c. 500-400 BCE (Laozi's Tao Te Ching)): The ultimate principle of Taoism. The source and pattern underlying all existence.
  • Olodumare / Olorun (African Traditions, Oral tradition; documented 19th-20th century CE): Supreme deity of the Yoruba tradition. Source of all Axé (divine power/life force).
  • Wakan Tanka (Indigenous Traditions, Oral tradition; documented c. 19th century CE): The supreme reality in Lakota spirituality.
  • The Dreaming / Tjukurpa (Indigenous Traditions, Oral tradition; 60,000+ years of continuous culture): The foundational reality in Aboriginal Australian spirituality.

Calendar systems (12)

  • Enochian Solar Calendar (Solar, c. 300–100 BCE (documented in 1 Enoch)): The 364-day calendar may be the calendar used by the original pre-exilic Israelites, before the Babylonian exile imposed the Babylonian lunisolar system.
  • Hebrew Lunisolar Calendar (Lunisolar, Babylonian exile period (c. 600–500 BCE); fixed calculation c. 359 CE): The Hebrew month names (Nisan, Tammuz, etc.) are Babylonian names adopted during the exile.
  • Jubilee Calendar (Solar Cycle, c. 160–150 BCE (Book of Jubilees); Leviticus 25 (Torah)): The Jubilee year involved: release of all Hebrew slaves, return of all land to original tribal owners, cancellation of debts.
  • Ancient Egyptian Civil Calendar (Solar, c. 2800 BCE (estimated)): The Egyptian civil calendar was the most precise annual calendar of the ancient world.
  • Zoroastrian Calendar (Fasli / Shahenshahi) (Solar, c. Achaemenid period (559–330 BCE)): Three variants exist: Qadimi (ancient — now about 1 month ahead of solar year due to no leap year correction), Shahenshahi (royal — about 1 month further ahead), and Fasli (seasonal — corrected to stay at equinox).
  • Ethiopian Orthodox Calendar (Ge'ez) (Solar (Julian Based), c. 4th century CE (adoption); older astronomical roots): Ethiopia is currently 7–8 years behind the Gregorian calendar because of a different calculation of the year of Christ's birth.
  • Gregorian / Julian Calendar (Solar, Julian: 46 BCE; Gregorian reform: 1582 CE): The 7-day week with Saturday Sabbath and Sunday worship preserves the tension between Jewish and early Christian practice.
  • Maya Long Count Calendar (Vigesimal (base 20), c. 400 BCE (earliest monuments)): The Maya calculated the synodic period of Venus to within 14 seconds of the modern value — using only naked-eye observation over centuries.
  • Hindu Lunisolar Calendar (Panchanga) (Lunisolar, Vedic period (c. 1500 BCE); current form c. 500 CE): The Hindu calculation of cosmic time is the most expansive of any tradition: one day of Brahma = 4.32 billion years (1 Kalpa).
  • Islamic Hijri Calendar (Lunar, 622 CE (Hijra — Prophet's migration from Mecca to Medina)): The Hijri calendar began with political migration (Hijra), not with creation or a divine event — making it unusual among religious calendars.
  • Celtic Calendar (Coligny Calendar) (Lunisolar, c. 2nd–1st century BCE (Coligny tablet); older oral tradition): The Coligny Calendar is the most complete surviving pre-Roman Celtic document.
  • Buddhist Calendar (Theravada) (Lunisolar, c. 3rd century BCE (standardization under Ashoka)): Tibetan Buddhist calendar is distinct — uses a 60-year animal-element cycle (Rab-jung) paralleling the Chinese zodiac.
